title: Intentions in prayer
hook: mystical meditations attached to the words of prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, gilgul: the kabbalists' teaching that a soul can return to finish its repair. Your line was souls continue. Whose way of doing things did you carry on? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

The Mishnah remembers a group it calls the pious ones of old. Before they prayed, it says, they would wait an hour, just to direct their hearts toward God. A whole hour of getting ready, before the first word. Some mornings, finding the right page is as far as anyone gets. But the question they were answering is an old and practical one. When the mouth says the words, where is the heart pointed? Later kabbalists answered it in fine detail. Today's word.
screen: `THE PIOUS ONES OF OLD.` → `AN HOUR BEFORE THE FIRST WORD.` → `WHERE IS THE HEART POINTED?`

segments.voice: Kavanot. The plural of kavanah: intention, the direction of the heart. Turn it four ways. First, the old rule. The Mishnah imagines someone reading the Torah aloud who reaches the passage of the Shema just as the time comes to say it. Does it count as their Shema? If they directed their heart, the Mishnah says, they have fulfilled it. Intention is what turns reading into prayer. Second, the kabbalists' kavanot. Luria and his students taught particular meditations to hold while saying the words of the prayers: divine names, the sefirot, the joining of one to another. A single word in the prayer book could carry a whole map. Some prayer books print these meditations beside the words, for those who pray with them. Third, a short doorway. Before doing a commandment, some Jews say a line that begins l'shem yichud, for the sake of the unification, naming the Holy One and the Shechinah, the indwelling presence from earlier in this stretch. In the kabbalists' language, the act joins what had been apart. Fourth, the Hasidic turn. Some Hasidic teachers taught a simpler kavanah for people who would never learn the full meditations: pray with your whole heart, cling to the words, let them carry you. Every one of these keeps the words the same. What changes is where the heart is pointed. Two people can say the same blessing over the same bread. One is reciting it. The other means it.
screen: `INTENTION MAKES READING PRAYER.` · `MEDITATIONS ON THE WORDS.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF UNIFICATION.` · `THE SIMPLER WAY: THE WHOLE HEART.` · then, large: `INTEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add one intention to a blessing. Settle, and breathe. If you say blessings, choose one you know well: over bread, over water, on waking. If you don't, choose a simple thank-you you say often. Before the words, pause. Ask what, exactly, you're pointing them toward. This glass of water. The person who cooked. The body that's thirsty. God, if you pray. Let one intention settle. Then say the words slowly, aloud or silently, with that intention riding on them. Rest in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
Kavanot. Intentions: meditations attached to the words of prayer, so the heart is pointed somewhere while the mouth speaks. Today's word.
Your line: intend. Today, before one ordinary thank-you or blessing, pause for a breath and decide what you mean by it. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Kavanah, directing the heart, is taught as part of Jewish prayer; in kabbalistic circles, some pray from prayer books that print Lurianic meditations beside the words, and some say a line beginning l'shem yichud before a commandment.

original.note: Hebrew: intentions; the singular, kavanah, is the direction of the heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: intention just means trying hard.
what it means: a direction of the heart, and in Kabbalah, particular meditations held on the words of prayer.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 2:1 and 5:1 on directing the heart, the Lurianic kavanot printed in some prayer books, and the formula l'shem yichud.

notes: Editor pass: removed 'astonishing' (empty uplift) and the unsourced 'in small letters'; howItsDone's 'part of all Jewish prayer' softened to 'taught as part of Jewish prayer' under the claims rule.
Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 paraphrased: the early pious ones waited one hour before praying to direct their hearts to God (the hour is stated in the Mishnah).
Mishnah Berakhot 2:1 paraphrased: one reading in the Torah when the time for Shema arrives has fulfilled the obligation if he directed his heart. Please confirm.

Lurianic kavanot described generally (divine names, sefirot, unifications), with Sha'ar ha-Kavanot as the source; the description of prayer books printing them (e.g. the Rashash siddur) is left without names or dates.
The l'shem yichud formula is described, not quoted or translated in full; please confirm 'naming the Holy One and the Shechinah' is accurate.
The Hasidic simpler kavanah is attributed to 'some Hasidic teachers'; please confirm this is fair and whether a specific source (e.g. a Baal Shem Tov teaching) should be cited.
The practice invites a blessing the listener already knows, or a plain thank-you; no new prayer is written.
